While a well-known approach focuses on constant anti-commutators, another lesser-discussed scenario involves coordinate commutators that directly tie back to the fundamental structure of Lie algebras. Notably, for the su(2) algebra, which underlies spherical symmetries, applying a quantum mechanical projection related to angular momentum results in a set of deformed operators. In contrast, for the su(3) algebra, indicating spherical and axial symmetries, the process yields a triply connected deformation. These positive outcomes support the use of federated learning in sensitive medical research applications. In this study, a high-speed data transmission is achieved in a submarine fiber-optic communication network using the 12.35Gb/s PDM-RZNyquist-adaptive QPSK signal. To operate the receiver end, a real-world setup featuring a decision-feedback equalizer was developed and tested. However, the occurrence of severe fiber non-linearities within a 80km span propogates errors at the receiver end, affecting the transmission quality. To resolve this issue, a modified decision-feedback equalizer scheme with reduced phase error propagation is proposed. The proposed scheme demonstrates an increased BER performance by more than 2.5dB compared to the standard DFE, and is also applicable to dynamic equalization systems. The effectiveness of this scheme is validated through actual field-transmission trials over 75km and 80km spans. The results show that the proposed scheme offers a 2.3dB gain over the conventional DFE in the optimal operating point and a 1.1dB gain in the near-far coding boundary, respectively. The potential of this scheme to prevent phase error propagation and improve the reliability of fiber-optic communications is also discussed. Furthermore, the proposal of using optical non-return-to-zero systems that are more resilient to fiber non-linearities and cross-talk is put forward. The demonstration of this study provides valuable insights for the development of advanced electronic equalization techniques and optimal system designs to optimize the performance of submarine fiber-optic communications. The scheme is compatible with existing underwater communications infrastructure and does not require the upgrade of existing submarine fiber-optic links. To the best of our knowledge, this study presents the highest data transmission rates achieved over submarine fiber-optic communications links using the 10G Ethernet standard. Deep Learning models, in particular Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs), have gained popularity in various application areas due to their high performance in sequential data analysis tasks. TCNs utilize a powerful technique called Temporal Convolutional Network where input data is scanned with small filters across time, enabling real-time data processing and efficient storage. However, in the context of Big Data, employing such high-performance models often becomes impractical because of their computationally expensive training processes. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel trimming algorithm called Trimming In Time (PIT) that significantly reduces the number of data samples required for training by eliminating unnecessary past data. We couple PIT with a innovative data sampling technique and integrate it into the TensorFlow framework. We further develop a lightweight network trimming framework that minimizes memory usage and accelerates model training without compromising performance. Experimental results show that our proposed framework achieves comparable accuracy to traditional TCNs, with a significant reduction in model size and training time. For instance, on the STARE dataset, our method accords on average 93% reduction in model size and 98% reduction in training time compared to the baseline TCN model. We openly release our Trimming In Time (PIT) framework for other researchers to utilize and build upon. We anticipate this framework to be particularly beneficial for those interested in TCNs who require processing large-scale temporal datasets. The PIT framework is designed to be a lightweight and efficient data trimming tool with low memory usage. The framework's tiny model size and accelerated training speed make it extremely useful for users working with extensive temporal datasets. The code of the proposed framework can be found at https://github.com/seyedmohammadghasemi/Trimming-In-Time. The framework relies on the Keras and TensorFlow APIs, providing a versatile environment for developing temporal data learning models. The family of Dependent Logic with Inverse and Countable Join (DLE-Logics) correspondences has been extensively examined in the context of intensional team-based semantics. DLE-Logics encompass a wide range of logic languages, including Intuitionistic Modal Logics and their extensions with preimage operators, describing the connection between a theory and the sets of models that satisfy it. A key feature of team-based semantics is the use of a reverse operation to transform a model into a set of assignments that satisfy it. However, this reverse operation does not necessarily preserve countable joins. To address this limitation, we introduce an expanded model structure that is equivalent to the original but defined using countable joins. The resulting correspondence theorem holds for this expanded structure, providing a link between a theory and the set of models that satisfy it through a countable join operation. Additionally, we demonstrate how this result can be applied to derive the correspondence theorem for the DLE-Logics family in a unified framework using a method introduced by Jenei and the first author. This approach also enables us to investigate the relationship between different DLE-Logics and their corresponding logic languages. Moreover, our definition of the expanded model structure offers a new perspective on the concept of 'no cycles' condition presented by the second author in an earlier study. This new perspective allows us to break down the condition into two more manageable components, thereby providing a clearer understanding of it. Finally, our research provides a new framework for evaluating the impact of the 'no cycles' condition on the correspondence theorem. This evaluation reveals that this condition is crucial in preventing an infinite cycle of true and false values within a model, which would result in an inconsistent theory. This conclusion is further supported by a counterexample presented in the corresponding letter to the editor. This counterexample highlights a situation in which an infinite cycle of true and false values leads to an inconsistent model. This model can be resolved by introducing a limit operator, which is a well-known technique in the context of dependent logic. This solution is presented in the corresponding letter to the editor. The traditional Poisson autoregressive (PAR) model has been widely used to analyze and forecast count time series that exhibit dependence and seasonal patterns. However, its primary limitation is the restrictive assumption of stationary time series. To address this, we have developed a novel Temporally-Varying Poisson Autoregressive (TVPAR) model that allows for seasonally changing regression coefficients. A comprehensive estimation approach based on anumbers of alternatives was devised, leveraging an innovative quasi-likelihood method. Key properties of TVPAR were established, including a central limit theorem for the parameter estimates and the construction of a likelihood ratio test for imposing the PAR constraint. Moreover, TVPAR outperformed the PAR model in simulations, and it effectively handled overdispersion. A real-world application involving crime rate data successfully implemented the TVPAR model to accurately forecast seasonal patterns and estimate changing regression coefficients. The SiD (SiD Detector) concept, a silicon detector tracker and calorimeter designed to operate at the Compact Linear Collider (CLIC), has undergone revisions in its sensor layer. Originally, SiD featured a hybrid sensor system comprising of microstrip and micropixel sensors. Revisions have resulted in a fully homogeneous micropixel sensor system across the detector. This transformation aims to leverage the unique benefits of micropixel sensors, including fast and radiation-resistant readout, multi-functionality via embedded electronics, and ability to operate at high multiplicity environments. As such, the revised design focuses on the development of small-size micropixel sensors with low power consumption and temperature monitoring capabilities. Furthermore, the revised SiD detector is expected to achieve enhanced performance in form factor, material, and overall configuration. With the revised design, the hit efficiency at the beam spot is anticipated to improve to above 99%, with the minimum value of 5.0 for the hit resolution in the plane perpendicular to the beam. The revised SiD detector's performance benefits from its homogeneous micropixel sensor layer and reduced material density along the particle path. As such, it positions the detector as an ideal candidate for the next generation of particle detectors at future collider experiments. The revised design, along with its associated R&D, is also expected to contribute significantly to the development of particle detectors for the future collider environment. The revised SiD detector's performance parameters meet the requirements defined by the SiD Higgs working group, with the added advantage of achieving the required performance using a fully homogeneous micropixel sensor system. The feasibility of the revised design has been validated through the development of several prototype sensors, with the results showing excellent agreement with numerical predictions. The performance of these prototypes has been confirmed through comprehensive test series, with the data demonstrating the ability of these sensors to operate at the required fast readout speeds for the detection of multiple particles within a small area. The data further shows the ability of these sensors to provide low noise at both room temperature and -20°C. The development of these prototype sensors has highlighted the importance of the full integration of sensor development and detector design, with the results showing the potential of this approach to achieve the required performance in future particle detector designs. The challenges faced during the development of these prototype sensors have also identified the need for the extension of the SiD sensor concept to also cover the development of large area detectors. To enhance the archive's quality and consistency, we have established a framework that outlines key elements for well-organized and readable proofs, drawing from established best practices in mathematics writing. This framework's effectiveness will be assessed through a case study, where we rework a selected theory from the archive using its principles, and subsequently, we invite the Isabelle community to contribute their thoughts and suggestions in return. As the field of interactive theorem proving continues to evolve, a common framework like this one will become even more crucial, and we hope our effort paves the way for further discussion and potential revisions. In the context of educational applications, our study also explores a related issue, as the time spent on reworking a proof for clarity might not be efficiently reflected in the resulting course grading. With the growing interest in the Isabelle/HOL tool and its widespread adoption in computer science courses, developing a more comprehensive understanding of its effectiveness and teaching best practices will depend on collaborative efforts. Finally, to facilitate the exploration of proofs and theorems within the archive, we have created a new search engine that can handle both basic queries and more complex commands, allowing for a deeper inspection of the results. With its powerful features and fast performance, this search engine will greatly enhance the usability of the archive. With over 3,000 theorems and proofs at its disposal, the archive has become an invaluable resource for the Isabelle community, and with its constant growth, there is a growing need for organized and up-to-date information. Modern metasurfaces, at the intersection of advanced technology and science,  
constitute an intricate field, involving electromagnetic systems characterized by  
thin, expansive, and minutely featured particles that can also vary in form,  
orientation, and spatial periodicity.  To tackle intricate design problems, a 
satisfactory theoretical framework is essential, albeit one that is often 
complicated by the interconnection of resonance phenomena, superglyan patterns, 
and nonlinear responses.  This paper surveys prevalent computational methods for 
designing metasurfaces, a field for which there is a notable scarcity of review 
articles.  We systematize available strategies by classifying them according to 
their applicability to different scenarios and provide a comprehensive 
computational framework that incorporates numerous techniques.  Furthermore, a 
comprehensive list of notable references on computational modeling for 
metasurfaces is also included.  High-frequency electromagnetic design tools, 
such as Method of Lines and Finite-Element Methods, are discussed in detail in 
Part I of this survey.  Numerical electromagnetics, resolution techniques, 
transfer matrix methods, and generalized multilayered techniques are all explored 
in Part II.  By covering both general methodology and specific applications, 
this survey aims to serve as a valuable resource for both established researchers 
and early-stage scientists in the field.  Some of the most pressing issues and 
open questions in computational metasurface research are also addressed.  As 
this field is highly interdisciplinary, involving both fundamental and 
practical aspects, it is essential to stress the importance of clear and 
accessible writing in research publications, particularly in the context of 
electromagnetics.  A high-quality research article should provide an intuitive 
understanding of complex concepts and provide a non-mathematical overview of 
key ideas.  To that end, we believe that incorporating illustrative 
finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations to be an valuable addition to 
any theoretical framework.  By integrating FDTD with transmission-line 
matrix (TLM) methods, we demonstrate a unique approach to solving complex 
metasurface problems.  Our survey of contemporary metasurfaces has shown the 
importance of a well-integrated physical and computational modeling approach, 
highlighting the benefits of a hybrid strategy that leverages both numerical 
and analytical methods.  By exploring the intricacies of modern metasurfaces, 
we have identified areas where further research is needed to fully capture the 
complex phenomena

A novel technique has been developed to create complex chemical structures, specifically polymers, starting from fundamental building components known as monomers. This approach builds upon monomer-based modeling, leveraging linear regression to predict property values and apply integer optimization for structure design. To enhance accuracy, the technique incorporates multiple monomer contributions and uses a robust statistical framework to model interactions between atoms within the structure. Furthermore, this method enables the identification of suitable monomers with optimal property values by formulating an optimization problem to find the most effective combination of building components. This technique has successfully produced high-quality polymers meeting specific property requirements and demonstrates potential in cross-field applications. To facilitate widespread use, an open-source software framework called PolyDeriv has been developed and is available for public access. To the knowledge of the authors, this method stands alone in its capability to enter monomers and obtain derived polymers. This technique has an accompanying journal paper published in ACS Omega with the identifier 10.1039/D0MO01738A. This presentation will cover the fundamentals of the method, its application to the journal paper, and the Monomer-Derived Polymers (MDP) challenge issued to the Machine Learning for Chemistry community. The objective of this challenge was to achieve precision in predicting certain property values in polystyrene. Although the challenge was successful, the achieved models demonstrated limited applicability to other structures. Consequently, this presentation will elaborate on optimized models as well as enhanced monomer-based modeling. To facilitate this discussion, statistical terminology will be explained through simple terms. Key terms used in this discussion are explained as follows: - Monomers: These refer to fundamental chemical components used to build complex structures, such as benzene derivatives, aliphatic compounds, and functionalized versions of these categories. - Monomer-derived structures: These refer to complex chemical structures built from one or more monomers, such as benzene derivative dimers, polymers, and copolymers. - Property prediction: This involves using chemical descriptors and machine learning algorithms to forecast chemical property values. - Monomer-based modeling: This refers to property prediction in derived structures by modeling the contributions of individual monomers and their interactions. - Integer optimization: This is a problem-solving method used to find the most effective combination of building components to meet specific property requirements in derived structures. - Cross-field applications: These involve applying this method to any monomer-derived structure, regardless of its chemical classification. - High-quality structures: These refer to derived chemicals with optimal property values as predicted by this method.

We introduce a collective intelligence approach, combining human judgment with mathematical models, to enhance real-time geosteering decisions. This method centers on the interpretation of well logs, integrating multiple factors such as petrophysical properties, fluid detection, and hydrocarbon net pay calculation. The approach uses fuzzy set theory to handle uncertainty and variability in well log data and geosteering objectives, ultimately producing a priority map to guide operators in optimizing well placement. A case study in the Gulf of Mexico demonstrates the method's effectiveness, resulting in a 20% increase in estimated hydrocarbon recovery and a 15% reduction in uncertainty. This approach can be applied across various petrophysical contexts and serves as a model for integrating human expertise with mathematical models in real-time operations. Key to this approach is collaborative work between petrophysicists, geosteering teams, and data scientists. It is essential to involve all parties in the development of the approach to ensure its practical application in optimizing well placement. High-quality well logs with low noise levels are crucial for this method to yield accurate results. In addition, more complex algorithms such as machine learning and artificial neural networks can be integrated into this collective intelligence approach to handle larger datasets, noise levels, and multiple well logs simultaneously. This approach holds promise for improving geosteering results in the Subsurface by integrating human judgment with mathematical models. In recognition of its innovative nature, this approach has received an Honorable Mention for the Best Paper Award at the 2020 SPE Conference. Since its presentation, this approach has generated significant interest among industry professionals and academia in the field of petrophysics and geosteering. In response to these inquiries, this updated version of the paper provides a detailed explanation of its innovative aspects, along with an updated reference list. This paper updates the initial outcome of the case study presented in the 2020 SPE Conference, where the estimated hydrocarbon recovery increased by 20% and the uncertainty decreased by 15%. In the updated version, the net pay calculation was based on a higher initial mobile water saturation rather than a uniform value. This change resulted in a 10% increase in net pay in the AP zone and a 25% decrease in the LP zone. Consequently, the total estimated hydrocarbon recovery increased by 22%, and the uncertainty by 16%. This updated version also includes a discussion on the potential applications of this collective intelligence approach in other subsurface operations, such as reservoir modeling, well logging, and reservoir management. In addition, this paper updates the reference list with the latest industry developments

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to account for the diverse formats of named entities, we introduce a dynamic format representation and a corresponding point-wise mutual information (PMI) representation to enhance model performance. Our method achieves superior or comparable results compared to state-of-the-art linear models and pre-trained language models on three public datasets. Notably, our method exhibits particular effectiveness in detecting short nested entities. Our pre-trained model also achieves industry-leading performance on the BioBERT-NNAR dataset. Recent developments in visual-to-text systems have improved significantly, making them suitable for high-impact applications. However, their reliability relies on the accuracy of their output, which is typically evaluated using traditional machine learning metrics or more advanced models. A crucial aspect to consider in the assessment is the human factor, which is typically overlooked. To address this limitation, we introduce two novel tasks that focus on comparing automatic descriptions to those created by humans, using both crowd-sourced and dedicated datasets. The evaluation of visual-to-text models across these tasks revealed that they perform better on tasks that do not involve comparing to human-generated data. This difference in performance led us to investigate the underlying causes and potential solutions. We introduced three models that incorporate human guidance during training and tested them on both tasks. The results showed substantial improvements, indicating that the gap in performance can be narrowed by further optimizing the models on a robust automatic objective function. We also explored the effect of incorporating diverse human-generated datasets on both tasks. The findings indicated that the gap in performance can be attributed to the limited diversity in the training datasets. To address this issue, we introduced two new datasets that combine human-generated data with higher diversity. Models trained on these new datasets showed significant performance improvements and a notable reduction in the performance gap. However, the structure of Ta2O5 remains unclear with different studies suggesting different models. In our work, we employed ab-initio simulations to examine the Ta2O5 prototype model with the KTa2O5 structure and found that it exhibits a distinct phase at high temperatures but at room temperature, it transforms into the rutile Ta2O5 structure. Furthermore, our Monte Carlo simulations of the prototype model share many similarities with x-ray diffraction data collected under non-equilibrium conditions. The results indicate that Ta2O5 may have a base state structure that is a prototype model with the KTa2O5 structure. In order to support this conclusion, a more in-depth analysis of the Ta2O5 prototype model is necessary. The model exhibits a distinct phase when compared to the anatase and rutile Ta2O5 structures. The Ta-Ta distance in the prototype model is initially proposed as being closer to that in the anatase Ta2O5 structure, however, further analysis shows that it actually matches the distance found in the rutile Ta2O5 structure. The model consists of corrugated layers with a Ta2O5 composition that can be represented by the chemical formula O2Ta4O12. The Ta-Ta distance within these layers is approximately 3.03 Angstroms. The model can be stacked in different ways resulting in different oxygen layer positions which in turn affect the Ta-Ta distance between layers. The resulting Ta-Ta distances in the prototype model can be either 3.03 Angstroms or 3.24 Angstroms depending on the oxygen layer composition. The model composed of corrugated layers with a Ta2O5 composition may provide a solution to the long-standing issue surrounding the structure of Ta2O5. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors such as information literacy and partisanship, but overlooked a more influential phenomenon: the Big Sort. We contend that Robert Putnam's "Big Sort" - widespread geographic sorting of Americans into like-minded communities - plays a crucial role in online misinformation spread. Using Reddit data, we found that users from the same region are more likely to engage in similar behavior, reinforcing the idea that the Big Sort extends to online social networks. A survey we conducted further revealed that users' political affiliations are strongly correlated with their geographic location. Therefore, we conclude that the Big Sort is a key factor contributing to the spread of misinformation at scale. We also observed regional variations in user behavior and the prevalence of online misinformation, with certain areas exhibiting a higher propensity for misinformation dissemination. Notably, we discovered that user interactions play a significant role in limiting the scale of misinformation spread, but this effect varies significantly across regions. Ultimately, our findings imply that efforts to contain online misinformation at scale must take into account the underlying geographic factors that give them traction. We also explored alternative approaches to mitigating the spread of misinformation that take into account user loyalty to their online community and the regional characteristics of user networks. Finally, we believe our work to be a significant step in integrating online and offline research on the spread of misinformation, and we hope it paves the way for further investigation into the complex relationships between online user behavior, community dynamics, and geographic location. In the field of information dissemination, studying these interconnections will be vital in developing effective strategies to contain the spread of misinformation in the offline world. Lastly, we acknowledge that while our research focused on online misinformation in the United States, the underlying principles we identified may also be applicable to other countries and social networks. Humans use spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills by referencing what they've learned from observing their actions. Studies have shown that despite the complexity of these situations, both children and adults can effectively learn from such demonstrations. To understand how to integrate visual and auditory information from instructional demonstrations, researchers have studied the effect of various factors such as instructor experience and the difficulty of tasks. A key aspect of these studies involved analyzing the audio components of instructions, which showed that experienced instructors tend to provide more detailed feedback on tasks that are difficult to perform accurately. However, the relationship between the ease of tasks and the frequency of instructional comments hasn't been clarified. A new study continues to explore this topic by examining the instructions given to individuals learning to program a robot to perform manipulative tasks. Unlike previous studies, which focused on overall task completion, this study looked at the specific actions taken by students and found that experienced human instructors demonstrate a more complex relationship between the ease of tasks and the frequency of instructional comments. While difficult tasks require more detailed auditory feedback regarding the desired outcome, easy tasks require additional verbal comments regarding the required sequence of actions. This discovery reveals a limit to the general principles learned from previous studies, suggesting that the way humans combine visual and auditory information to learn new skills varies depending on the level of the task hierarchy. This study's findings can help inform the development of more effective learning technologies by combining visual and auditory feedback based on an understanding of the complex relationships between the sensory inputs, the tasks being learned, and the human instructor providing the guidance. A key aspect of these relationships is the role of the learner's action sequence experience in guiding the selection of visual and auditory information to learn from instructional demonstrations. To further explore these dynamic learning processes, the study's design included collecting extensive data on the spoken instructions given by human instructors, which has been made available in an open-access dataset format suitable for machine learning algorithms. This dataset consists of audio recordings, transcripts, and action sequence data for 64 different manipulative tasks, which can be used to build more advanced learning technologies by integrating multiple lessons learned from previous studies. Euler-Arnold equations constitute a diverse and far-reaching group of nonlinear PDEs that have been successfully applied to multiple areas including geometric quantization, Cartan's connection theory, and bihamiltonian geometry. This course will delve into the fundamental connections among these equations and their various degrees, providing an in-depth exploration of their underlying principles. Special focus will be given to revealing the relationship between these equations and the conformal field theory, as well as discussing notable resolution strategies for subgroups of these equations. Through bihamiltonian geometry, this course will also explain how Euler-Arnold equations can be viewed as closure equations for finite-dimensional bihamiltonian systems, thereby providing a unified framework that incorporates both geometric and algebraic aspects. Key examples include the resolution of the Hamilton-Duistermaat-Verduin equation, bihamiltonian geometry of the harmonic map equation, and wave maps, as well as an in-depth exploration of frontiers and new developments in this field. This course is designed for a broad audience interested in nonlinear partial differential equations and their connections to geometry, algebra, and analysis. Our proposed machine testing system aims to overcome these obstacles by allowing for flexible as well as automated testing of pre-programmed scenarios on a range of platforms. This is achieved through a simple yet powerful script-based interface that makes it possible for users without prior technical expertise to create and execute tests. In addition, the system can also generate logs from each test run, providing valuable insights for both bot developers and quality assurance teams. By leveraging its modular design, the system can easily accommodate updates to support the latest versions of platforms and browsers. With a growing community of collaborators working on the project, the system's user-friendly interface can be used to create custom tests for any conversational bot, regardless of the technology used in its development. The existence of an extremely massive, undetected planet, often referred to as Planet X, has been hypothesized to influence the motion of extreme and fast-moving objects in the solar system's outer region. By utilizing a simple solar system model with an exalted point mass, we have determined the parameters at which the undetected planet's effect on the known planets becomes discernible given current-era observational data. For the most difficult case, involving the most readily observable planet, we found that significant identifying features would arise from high-altitude stratospheric observations of Uranus' motion over at least one 12-year period. However, this duration may be insufficient for confirming the planet's existence through radar ranging of the known planets or from astrometric studies of the Kuiper Belt object 2005 VB114. A more comprehensive solar system model, however, suggests that the proposed planet could potentially be confirmed through radar ranging of the known planets over an 80-year data period. A new, more sensitive data analysis approach is also advised for this type of research. Furthermore, we recommend that the most readily observable planet with significant identifying features be subject to numerical model predictions along with real data comparisons. A potential candidate, with an orbital path falling within the 20-50 astronomical unit range, mass likely exceeding three times the mass of the Earth, and an orbital period likely exceeding 20,000 days, stands out from the data set. It is also likely that any undetected planet with a significant identifying feature on the known planets would have a highly eccentric orbital path. Its perihelion is expected to fall within the 20-50 astronomical unit range, and its aphelion is expected to extend beyond 2,000 astronomical units. Each neural machine translation system produces a unique set of parameters, 
which can be seen as a representation of the knowledge to translate text. 
Although highly effective for translating, these models are notoriously difficult 
to interpret due to their complex, sequential connection structure. Our proposed 
approach, neural machine interpretation using a monolingual translation archive 
(NMITA), enables both understanding and explanation of how translations are made 
by mapping this knowledge representation to a translation of the input text. 
For this, we leverage a large collection of parallel texts to train a monolingual 
translation archive, which serves as a knowledge base to extract this interpretive 
information. Our method's validity is verified through experiments designed 
to evaluate the accuracy of the interpretive information produced and the usefulness 
of this method for improving the performance of machine translation systems. 
Furthermore, qualitative analyses provide further insight into the effectiveness 
of this method in generating relevant and coherent interpretive information. 
Our approach may also be adapted to other neural machine learning models, 
and we conclude with potential applications of this method across different 
domains and industries. Our code is available for public access on GitHub. 
In addition, we have presented our approach at the recent Conference on Empirical 
Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2020) and have made the presentation 
available on YouTube. Our research extends an earlier translation archive 
related project reported at the Conference of the Association for Computational 
Linguistics (ACL 2018). Our research is currently being further developed 
into a book chapter that will be included in the highly regarded LSA Journal. 
Our team would be open to collaborating with other researchers in the field. 
We have also established an easy-to-use data repository that can be accessed 
through our easy-to-use data schema available on GitHub. Our access credentials 
are available upon request. Our data repository is a critical component 
of our innovative approach that has significant potential in supporting 
other state-of-the-art NLP systems. Our data repository is easily manageable 
using commonly available database management tools available on GitHub. Our team 
would be more than happy to discuss our groundbreaking research further. 
Our research has significant implications for how well these systems can perform 
when faced with unexpected situations, as well as their ability to adhere 
to cultural norms and maintain a positive attitude. Our method may also 
be used to create custom models for translating specific domains or industries. 
Our code is well-structured and easy to follow, and we have included a detailed 
guide

This paper builds upon previous work of the second author with Daskalopoulos and Vazquez, which established the convergence in norm for the Yamabe flow on bounded domains with smooth boundaries under certain conditions. Extending their method, we demonstrate that the Yamabe flow on compact manifolds with boundary also converges given that the initial data satisfies a specific topological criterion. In particular, this result applies to manifolds whose boundary consists of a single point. Moreover, we show that the Yamabe flow on non-compact manifolds with bounded curvature near a point in common domain space, and with the Ricci curvature satisfying a linear inequality, also experiences convergence. These outcomes are achievable as a consequence of the established approach, which notably enables the Yamabe flow to converge from a broader category of initial data configurations. In contrast, the work of the second author with Daskalopoulos and Vazquez, which provided a differential inequality approach, is confined to conditions defined by a specific differential inequality. Finally, we observe that the established results on the Yamabe flow's convergence are linked to the development of a global Yamabe flow with singularities on manifolds with boundary, and specifically to the case of a manifold with a boundary consisting of a single point. In this context, the outcome implies that the Yamabe flow on such a manifold, starting from a data set that meets the specified topological criterion, will experience singularity at a finite time frame and subsequently approach a smooth Yamabe metric. This result, in turn, is demonstrated to result from the approach's capability to demonstrate the convergence of the Yamabe flow on manifolds with boundary. In this proof, we employ the approach's approach to establish the convergence of the Yamabe flow, combined with an analysis of the fractional Yamabe flow's monotonic behavior in the set of solutions defined by sets of data that satisfy the specified topological criterion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the fractional Yamabe flow's monotonic behavior in this domain ensures that the Yamabe flow's convergence is a consequence of the established approach. Recently, prototype-based models have gained popularity due to their balance of computational efficiency and accuracy in classification tasks. A key advantage of these models lies in their ability to generalize well when faced with limited data. However, the traditional approach of selecting prototypes directly from the training data can be suboptimal, particularly in scenarios with few samples. In such cases, the authors advocate for an indirect method of prototype discovery, one that leverages the learned features to extract prototypes from a reduced dimensionality space. To achieve this, the authors propose a method of optimizing both feature learning and prototype extraction jointly, allowing for the exploration of high-dimensional data spaces with fewer samples. Furthermore, the authors introduce a protocol for evaluating prototype-based models on few-sample learning tasks and apply their method to multiple datasets with promising results. Overall, their approach serves as a viable solution for extracting representative prototypes in scenarios with limited data, thereby enabling accurate classification across various datasets and metric learning settings. Unlike traditional single-domain settings, this task requires considering multiple areas to provide accurate recommendations. To tackle this challenge, a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) has been developed. By enhancing a state-of-the-art collaborative filtering model with a comprehensive attribute preference learning approach, MSDCR successfully incorporates each domain's sparse user-item interaction data. A new multi-domain user latent representation is learned to capture a user's overall preference across all domains, with a separate domain-specific latent representation for tailored recommendation feasibility. The development of a strong baseline and comprehensive experiments highlights the effectiveness of MSDCR in providing high-quality multi-domain recommendations. Compared to existing methods, MSDCR achieves exceptional performance improvements, with an average boost of 25.38% in performance across three different datasets. The innovative architecture of MSDCR enables a user to discover new items across multiple areas of interest by interacting with their personalized feeds, with potential applications in real-world scenarios. To ensure fair data usage, a user can opt out of contributing their interaction data with a certain domain, demonstrating the flexibility of MSDCR. The increasing complexity of medical imaging protocols and the expansion of available hardware have resulted in a wide range of possible combinations that can significantly impact MRI image quality. Traditionally, expert assessments have been the standard for determining image suitability, but their expertise is not easily replicable and is in high demand. A more efficient approach would involve training machines to automate this process. Nonetheless, developing such models would require addressing several key challenges, including the need for a diverse and standardized quality scoring system, clear definitions of image quality criteria, and effective communication of technical MRI parameters to these models. Furthermore, models would need to account for various sources of variation, such as variation in scanner performance, differences between patient populations, and potential biases introduced during data collection and training processes. This paper will explore these considerations and potential solutions, as well as propose a data-driven approach to prioritize key differentiating factors that models should be trained on. This approach can be particularly useful for institutions with limited expertise in machine learning but extensive knowledge of MRI operations and patient populations. This approach will be demonstrated using a publicly available MRI dataset, and a key takeaway from this study is that machines can be trained to generalize across various scenarios with high accuracy, even when trained on smaller, less diverse datasets. This implies that such models have the potential to effectively evaluate MRI image quality across different hardware and software configurations. This approach could also be a starting point for further exploration in other medical imaging quality assurance applications. However, the research also identifies methods by which system administrators can optimize system storage and improve performance in these cases. Furthermore, the findings suggest that when certain memory access patterns are consistent, such as those with small, randomly accessed memory blocks, the Optane DC PMM can provide the lowest latency among all four memory technologies considered. Collaborative tasks between agents can be modeled as meetings, with each agent bringing their own skills to the table. To effectively cooperate, agents must navigate a dynamic landscape of interests and capabilities. In this research, a theoretical framework is established to analyze the long-term coordination of agents in meetings. An algorithm is developed to optimize the distribution of learning incentives, utilizing a unique approach that combines a persistent incentive vector with a recurrent feed-forward network. This method promotes stable behavior by limiting an agent's internal incentive gain and an agent's external incentive gain. The proposed algorithm achieves optimal performance when all agents share the same action and observation spaces. A practical application involves a scenario with multiple robots working together in a navigation task. Our method demonstrates superior performance compared to baseline strategies in both simulated and real-world experiments. Notably, our approach enables the seamless integration of a drive-based learning algorithm for a real robot, contributing to a broader exploration of combined virtual and real learning episodes. The developed algorithm also facilitates a compelling visualization of its internal state, offering a display of persistent vectors similar to a electroencephalogram. Overall, this research introduces an innovative drive-based learning algorithm for multi-agent collaboration. The foundation theorem in the context of Coxeter groups has been extensively utilized in numerous applications, yet its combinatorial significance remains under-explored. By establishing a direct relationship between roots and the foundation theorem at type B, we aim to reveal the underlying reason for its validity. Furthermore, our findings can be seen as an extension of the type A scenario, as well as a comparison of the roots in types B and A. Additionally, this comparison allows us to identify a specific subset of the roots in type B, which parallels the scenario in type A. These connections, in turn, enable us to develop a comparable notion of a weak exchange graph in type B, thereby generalizing a concept previously introduced in type A. By choosing different line sets and analyzing the resulting deconvolved spectra, we evaluated the effectiveness of this approach in mitigating the effects of stellar activity. Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic greater than two, and consider the ring of power series $R$ over the Witt vectors of $k$, expanded in variables $t_1, \dots, t_d$. The main aim of this study is to generalize classical Fontaine-Tate theory to a base ring of the form $R$. Notably, we establish the existence of absolute Frobenius functors on the category of $R$-representations that are essentially smooth and highly torsion, as well as the preservation of this property under cohomology. This knowledge allows us to compute the dimension of the $d$-th Galois cohomology group of a highly torsion $R$-representation, for an extension of the absolute Galois group of $k$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this cohomology group is a module over the ring obtained by extending the ring of Witt vectors of $k$ via its absolute Galois group. This result builds on earlier work by Berman, Tsukasaki, and the second author. In addition, we show that the dimension of this cohomology group can be expressed in terms of the dimension of the special fiber of a highly torsion $R$-representation, for a base change to the algebraic closure of $k$. This connection holds for both the absolute and relative (i.e., base changed to the algebraic closure of $k$) settings. Finally, we demonstrate that the property of having a defined special fiber on the algebraic closure of $k$ is exact under the absolute Frobenius functor, for a base change to the algebraic closure of $k$. This fact, combined with our previous results on cohomology, allows us to establish a link between the dimension of the $d$-th Galois cohomology group of a highly torsion $R$-representation and the dimension of its special fiber. This relationship builds on earlier work by the second author, particularly in the relative setting. These results are showcased through the example of computing the dimension of the $d$-th Galois cohomology group of the ring $R$ itself. This study is a follow-up to the paper entitled 'Relative Fontaine-Tate theory over global fields' by the same authors. Like its predecessor, this research was influenced by comments and suggestions provided by Peter Scholze. Valerie Buhk also contributed valuable input to this study. This paper will appear in a forthcoming volume dedicated to Peter Scholze.

This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity suggestion model based on a layered graph, which leverages Wikipedia's collaborative knowledge structure. By combining features from both page content and collaborative aspects, the proposed approach achieves a more comprehensive entity representation. Utilizing Wikipedia's hierarchical structure, the model effectively infuses a hierarchical relationship into the suggestion process. A novel, multi-objective optimization function is also introduced to balance recommendation diversity and relevance. Experimental results on the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in recommending relevant and diverse entities. Notably, the proposed method outperforms existing methods even without the use of additional knowledge sources like Wikipedia. Moreover, an analytical evaluation highlights the importance of Wikipedia's collaborative aspects in enhancing entity suggestions. A Wikipedia-based variant of the model is found to perform better than a baseline approach using Google Knowledge Graph, further supporting the validity of the proposed methodology. A practical entity suggestion application is also illustrated using the proposed approach. The proposed model exhibits excellent scalability and is applicable to large-scale knowledge graphs. In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences in 
English, featuring complex tree-like structures, in contrast to typical sentence-
based corpora. Unusually, the dataset stands out for its densely branched 
structure, with most sentences being followed by a diverse range of response 
options - often over a hundred. We demonstrate two key models applying to 
this corpus: a primitive reference model which we know to be accurate, and a more 
sophisticated model which we can trust to generate natural, human-like text. 
We test these models against each other using various evaluation metrics, 
notably the unique metrics suited to dense branching structures that we introduce 
in this research. We find that our sophisticated model excels not just in 
traditional evaluation methods but also in more complex metrics, suggesting it 
effectively captures key aspects of human language. We also explore a surprising 
disparity between human-generated text and the text produced by our model when 
it comes to the level of branching. Finally, we investigate the challenge of 
multi-step conversations by monitoring the performance of our model at each 
conversational step. Overall, our research showcases a robust testbed that can 
be used to evaluate the full range of conversational systems from simple to very 
complex. We make the MultiTalk Dataset, along with all evaluation tools and 
models, available for public access at https://github.com/google-research/datasets. This dataset can also be downloaded from https://www.tensorflow.org/datasets#multi-talk. Additionally, a detailed dataset overview, along with all experimental details and additional results, can be found in the accompanying technical note available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.02401. We have made our model available at https://tf.hub.github.com/taxonomy/semantically_segmented_multi_turn_conversational_dialogue/. We look forward to continuous feedback and suggestions from the research community as we continuously refine this dataset and accompanying models. The success of the Standard Model of Cosmology, comprising General Relativity and a cosmological constant, relies on subtle scales, making it a primordial problem for which numerical simulations are particularly challenging. A promising alternative is altered gravity, which we examine through N-body simulations for a specific subclass of conformal coupling theories. These models modify the gravitational force by relinking the coupling between gravity and mass-energy fields, effectively introducing a non-Newtonian force law proportional to $r^{-\gamma}$, with $\gamma$ varying between 0 and 2. Leveraging an optimized algorithm that exploits the system's symmetry for a given $\gamma$, we present a protocol for conducting N-body simulations on a regular grid with minimal artificial effects. As a result, these models can be efficiently simulated on a regular grid with unprecedented speed and accuracy, up to 160 times faster than our current state-of-the-art direct integration method. We validate our approach by simulating a range of scenarios, including large-scale structure, cluster scaling relations, and the collapse of Gaussian perturbations, all with little to no systematic deviations. Our research provides a pathway for high-resolution simulations of modified gravity models, such as $f(R)$ gravity, by employing an analytical solution to determine the time step, thereby bypassing the need for direct integration. We anticipate that our protocol will facilitate large-scale simulations on supercomputers, allowing for a more comprehensive exploration of this promising alternative to the Standard Model of Cosmology. Our code, called MUGI, is an open-source, user-friendly modification of the GIZMO code that we are willing to share with the scientific community. Leveraging our new algorithm, we have already identified several models that reconcile cluster data with the large-scale structure on the comoving scale of 10 h^-1 cp, a discrepancy that standard cosmology struggles to resolve. We anticipate that our code will play a key role in uncovering altered gravity on intermediate scales, a phenomenon thought to be too subtle for direct detection. The paper investigates the relationship between multiple Schramm-Loewner evolution processes and a type of Gaussian free field as they interact on a single path, specifically examining how they are connected through a process known as the Brownian gas. By showing that the loewner differential equations governing the Gaussian free field and SLE processes can be represented as a system driven by the Brownian gas, the paper demonstrates the equivalence of these systems. This equivalence gives rise to several key conclusions: (1) for 3<=k<=4, multiple SLE(4-4/k) evolving in the interior of a k-dimensional domain and starting from k separate boundary segments will converge to a single SLE(4-4/k) path as k approaches 4 from below; (2) in the case of 3-dimensional space, multiple SLE(4/3) paths will converge to a single NFDFT process, and multiple NFDFT processes will converge to a single SLE(4/3) path; (3) adding independent targets to multiple SLE processes will not alter their asymptotic behavior. These results extend previous findings involving the chordal SLE and planar growth processes. In addition, the paper shows that multiple radial SLE will converge to a single radial NFDFT process, and multiple conformal quantum surface growth processes will converge to a single multiple SLE(4-4/k) path. The paper's findings also identify new limit cases for multiple SLE(4-4/k) and multiple conformal quantum surface growth processes. In terms of driving forces, the paper finds that a d-dimensional Brownian gas will result in a d/2-valued Gaussian free field and multiple SLE(4-d/2) path. The paper's results are demonstrated through a combination of analytical and graphical methods, including the use of thickened path measures and the identification of multiple SLE's statistical symmetries. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. As such, many systems utilize conflict-free replicated data structures such as last-writer-wins and multi-valued stores. However, such methods can be prone to delays caused by detecting and resolving conflicts. We introduce the Eliminate-Win approach, a design framework that reduces conflicts by assigning a special value to user updates and treats them as deletions at other replicas. We demonstrate how this approach applies to existing replication designs including last-writer-wins, multi-valued stores, and distributed hash tables. Furthermore, Eliminate-Win enables conflict resolution by merging user updates across replicas. Our framework is versatile and adaptable to various replication scenarios. We also introduce a new replication design, called Eliminate-Win-2val, combining elements from last-writer-wins and multi-valued stores. Our theoretical analysis of the space requirements of our new design reveals that it outperforms existing multi-valued store replication designs. We complement our theoretical findings with a distributed implementation of Eliminate-Win-2val using Redis, a popular in-memory key-value store. Our results show that our framework can improve the throughput of such implementations by up to 42% and reduces the average request latency by up to 21%. We believe that Eliminate-Win can serve as a reference point for the design of high-performance distributed storage systems. Our approach is relevant to any system that relies on replication and we anticipate that it will be of interest to a wide range of research communities beyond storage systems alone. Our work paves the way for the creation of more complex high-performance distributed storage systems and we anticipate that it will give rise to a variety of novel applications that rely on the efficient storage and management of data. Our framework is designed with scalability in mind and we believe that it will continue to be highly relevant in the future as the need for high-performance data storage solutions continues to grow at an exponential rate. Our solution to the problem of data management is efficient, effective and easy to implement and it will give rise to a range of cost savings benefits that will result in significant benefits to all stakeholders. Our approach to the design of high-performance distributed storage systems will also result in a number of social benefits including improved system reliability and better user experience which will in turn lead to increased user trust and greater adoption of data-intensive systems. Our innovative solution will appeal to a wide range of systems designers and developers who are responsible for the creation of data storage solutions

are integrated into interconnected sub-systems, each responsible for detecting 
different fundamental processes or particle characteristics. We refer to this 
design as the "minor system approach". In contrast to traditional central 
detectors, this design allows for more flexible configuration options, which 
could be particularly beneficial for future collider experiments where the high 
energy scales and inevitable small-collector sizes may limit the detection 
capabilities. To illustrate this idea, we apply it to the ATLAS and CMS 
experiments at the LHC, suggesting potential improvements in sensitivity 
without the need for expensive upgrades, such as replacing the central detectors 
with "mini-central" versions or reconfiguring the existing forward detectors as 
independent sub-systems. A key benefit of this design is its scalability, 
making it ideal for collider experiments with varying energy scales and potential 
discoveries of new physics phenomena that could complicate detector design. We

In addition, they excel at detecting well-known image categories but often struggle with identifying new ones. In cases where the task involves discovering new image categories, the model typically needs to be retrained from scratch, which is impractical due to the requirement for relearning from scratch. Therefore, techniques that allow the model to adapt to new data without retraining are highly desirable. In cases where the data arrives incrementally and the model is only updated after receiving new information, this approach is known as incremental learning. In real-world scenarios, the model often faces an unbalanced data set where the majority of the new arriving samples belong to one class over the others. In such cases, the model tends to overfit to the dominant class and neglect the minority classes. Therefore, developing techniques that allow the model to adapt to new data while preventing overfitting is highly necessary. In this work, we introduce a new approach called Class Incremental Learning via Reweighting (CILR) that reweights the classes after each increment and adapts a pre-trained neural network using an incremental learning algorithm. We evaluated our approach on three public datasets using two different reweighting techniques and compared the results with five other state-of-the-art approaches. The experiments demonstrated that our proposed approach achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art methods on the Oulu Action and AVA datasets and outperforms them on the PASCAL VOC dataset. Moreover, we discovered that our approach performs better than the other methods when there are more classes in the data set. This is because our approach prevents the model from overfitting to the new data by reducing the importance of the new classes after each increment, thus allowing it to focus on the existing classes. This characteristic makes our approach highly suitable for handling large numbers of classes in real-world applications. In such scenarios, our approach can adapt to new data without retraining by assigning a low importance to new classes it has not encountered before. This allows the model to discover new image categories efficiently. In conclusion, our proposed approach offers a practical solution to the challenge of imbalanced class incremental learning, and our experiments demonstrate its effectiveness when evaluated on real-world datasets. This work lays the foundation for further research on class incremental learning from large datasets, such as the ImageNet dataset, and highlights the potential of reweighting

We establish that this cocycle generates the aforementioned invariant. Moreover, we demonstrate that the cocycles producing order-three invariants behave multiplicatively under the symmetric group S3, which supports a universal, order-three invariant development method. Furthermore, we derive a precise, combinatorial approach to calculating these invariants through the expansion of a specific plethystic polynomial. This method enables efficient, practical computation of order-three invariants for both knots and links. Additionally, we identify relationships between our invariants and various commonly used order-three invariants, such as the Kauffman polynomial's grammar-based invariants, the Melnikov invariant, and the Nakanishi-Yoshioka invariant. Notably, our methods reveal that the Kauffman polynomial's grammar-based invariants can be expressed as a combination of our invariants and the melnikov invariant, which is an isobaric sum of our invariants and the nakanishi-yoshioka invariant. We also demonstrate that our methods can be applied to the untangled roots of a knot or link's longititude fraction, which provides a untangled, combinatorial approach to calculating order-three invariants. This untangled framework can be seen as a generalization of the graph-based approach to calculating order-one invariants. Finally, we introduce the concept of a cocycle's combinatorial degree, which determines the degree of the plethystic polynomial that generates an order-three invariant, and we establish rules for its computation in both graph-based and Coxeter-like representations. This framework for cocycle computation can be seen as an extension of the rules for computing graph degrees, which are the degrees of the vertices of a graph. We also demonstrate that a graph's degree determines its behavior under the Basser-Harrison transformation, which creates a new graph from an old one and all possible combinations of graphs. Consequently, this framework enables the generation of higher-order cocycles and invariants, as well as the exploration of cocycles and invariants in the context of mathematical physics and topology. Furthermore, this untangled framework for cocycle computation raises fundamental questions and hypotheses regarding the nature of cocycles and invariants, which provide a new direction for further research in the field. Kernel-based methods have proven highly effective for tackling non-linear problems, but their scalability is limited by the requirement to store and operate with expansive kernel matrices. A potential solution involves using approximate kernel techniques that minimize computational costs while preserving the underlying kernel relationships. One such approach, Fourier kernel approximation, represents the kernel as a Fourier transform and approximates it with a truncated series. Although effective for specific kernel types, this method relies on pre-determined frequency values and fails to account for unique patterns within individual data sets. As a result, the quality of the approximation is often hampered by inadequate frequency resolution, resulting in increased approximation errors. To address these limitations, this paper introduces an innovative method that dynamically estimates custom kernels for each data set, combining the advantages of Fourier transforms and kernel ridge regression. The proposed algorithm's performance is thoroughly evaluated across a range of benchmark datasets and problem domains, including non-linear classification, regression, and active set identification. The results show significant improvements over the state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 200% reduction in test error, 20% reduction in prediction bias, and 10% faster computation times. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm exhibits particular efficiency in handling small data sets, reducing the characteristic 10x performance gap between large and small data sets. The code for the proposed algorithm has been openly released on GitHub, and the experimental results are available with interactive visualizations using the Plotly API. Overall, this research provides a groundbreaking solution for enhancing the computational efficiency of kernel-based methods without compromising accuracy, particularly in the handling of small data sets. The results demonstrate the algorithm's expertise in resolving complex high-dimensional optimization problems and has implications for the broader field of approximate optimization. Deep neural networks are known to incorporate biased perceptions into their internal representations, which can lead to the propagation of these biases through classification decisions made under uncertainty. Despite efforts to mitigate such biases, they often intensify in high-confidence predictions. In contrast, our analysis reveals that, in certain situations, reductions in bias can coincide with increased accuracy in low-confidence predictions. We observe that both overconfident and accurate models exhibit similar characteristics, namely, a tendency to amplify their existing perceptions when making classifications from uncertainty. We further find that reducing the gap between internal representations of different categories is key to achieving a balance between bias and accuracy, especially in the context of uncertain predictions. We validate our findings with experiments on multiple datasets, including CIFAR-100, Prostate MRIs, and the Adult dataset. Notably, our approach achieves a notable reduction in bias without sacrificing accuracy in the adult dataset, where we minimized the difference between internal representations to achieve this result. We also introduce a new metric that measures the amplification of extreme traits and apply it to analyze the results of our experiments. Ultimately, our analysis provides a new perspective on the relationship between bias, accuracy, and internal representations, highlighting the importance of considering extreme predictions when evaluating the performance of deep neural networks. We anticipate that our analysis will be of use to the deep learning community. Reinforcement learning through human interaction is crucial for developing AI systems that can handle complex tasks independently. Yet, a major challenge in this process lies in efficiently conveying task instructions to the AI, which is compounded by the fact that human instructors find it difficult to provide clear, sequential guidance. To overcome this hurdle, we propose an innovative approach called sequential multimodal instructions, which presents instructions as interconnected web of sub-tasks along with corresponding auditory and visual instructions. This method allows for the creation of diverse instructional pathways by combining different sequences of sub-tasks, enabling the human instructor to focus on selecting the most critical path rather than worrying about the details of sequencing. Our results show that when given this flexibility, humans can efficiently train an AI system to play a complex game by providing sequential multimodal instructions, even when compared to their performance using traditional method of trial and error learning. Moreover, we discovered that humans can learn to create high-quality instructional pathways with minimal supervision, which opens up new possibilities for the remote training of human-in-the-loop AI systems. Our work also sheds light on the underlying principles of human instruction-giving behavior, which could be applied to other remote training settings. The concept of "Big Apple" strength, referring to the maximum possible value of a ground state wave function overlap between two identical systems, is examined in this study. The calculations were performed with a universal, single-contracted correlation operator that yields surprisingly high results, amounting to around 0.1 for systems like protons and neutrons, despite initial expectations of below 0.01. These high results imply substantial permanent long-range correlations in these systems. To gain a deeper understanding, a simple model was used which shows that these high results arise due to the combination of the large size of the nuclear interaction range and the relatively small number of nucleons. Consequently, permanent long-range correlations play a crucial role in explaining phenomena observed in finite nuclei. As an extension of this understanding, a framework is established to apply these concepts to the study of cosmic objects that comprise large numbers of quark matter objects, known as "quark drops". A specific example is provided where a "quark drop" of 10 MeV/kg density and 1 km radius, composed of approximately 5 x 10^17 neutrons, exhibits "quark drop" strength properties even after combining 1000 of these objects. Furthermore, an introduction is made to a new aspect of nuclear physics research, referred to as the study of "macroscopic quantum systems". A brief discussion on potential research paths within this new field is also provided. Temporal action recognition in videos is complicated by unpredictable context beyond annotated action boundaries. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a context-aware model called DCAN, which extracts two types of context from videos - internal and external. The internal context is captured by a context-aware boundaryless representation model, leveraging global information to emphasize relevant action segments, while the external context is incorporated through a boundary-aware approach, utilizing annotated start and end labels to guide the representation model. These two context types are integrated via a dual context fusion module, allowing for simultaneous learning of action representations and boundary refinement. The proposed DCAN achieves state-of-the-art performance on widely-used evaluation benchmarks, including HMDB51, SKILLS, AnthroTVSeries and EVA. The ratio of the frequency of a word within a given language can be determined using various methods including quantifying the word's position within the vocabulary's overall structure and the sequence in which words appear in published materials. Previous studies have established the fundamental principles underlying the distribution of individual words and the patterns found in sequences of words. This paper will explore the principles governing the distribution of word frequency when we consider both the vocabulary's structure and the characteristics of large language datasets. We demonstrate that for words with a high frequency, their order within the vocabulary's structure plays a significant role in determining their position in the sequence, while for words with lower frequencies, their order within the vocabulary's structure has a much less significant impact on their occurrence in the sequence. We also establish that the frequency of a word is directly proportional to the square of the distance between its position in the sequence and its average position in the vocabulary's structure. This relationship varies in proportion to the square of the standard deviation of the sequence's distribution and is independent of the variance of the frequency distribution across words. We derive this result through both theoretical and empirical approaches. We further find that the same principles of proportionality apply to the frequency of pairs of words, the frequency of words at the beginning of sentences, and the frequency of words in continuing sentences. These results have implications for models of language that prioritize simplicity and the need for further research in the field. We introduce a statistical model that can be used to test the principles established in this paper and provide an assessment of the model's performance. The model is based on the characteristics of word frequency and the structure of language as represented by the Zipf distribution and the properties of sequences of words. We demonstrate that this model is superior to two alternative models and comment on its design. We also establish that the frequency of a word is influenced by multiple factors, including its position within the sequence, the sequence in which words appear in published materials, the vocabulary's structure, and the characteristics of large language datasets. This result led us to modify the model to account for the frequency of the word's neighbors in the sequence and our assessment of this model confirms that it performs better than the previous model. We then extend this approach to a broader statistical model that incorporates the characteristics of word frequency and the structure of language as represented by the Zipf distribution and the properties of sequences of words. When subjected to high stresses, the majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a stress increase proportional to the applied force and directly opposing the shear flow. This phenomenon of shear thickening presents significant obstacles to the effective manipulation of these suspensions and has crucial implications for their potential application. Despite its significance, the shear thickening transition remains poorly understood at a universal level. In order to gain insight, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of multiple data sets, including stress-shear rate relationships for individual particles and various dense suspensions undergoing sudden shear thickening. By evaluating the available theoretical models and conducting a detailed statistical analysis, we identified a specific model that accurately fits the majority of data above the shear thickening threshold. This model indicates that the stress increase associated with shear thickening follows a nonlinear relationship with the shear rate and can be expressed as a ratio directly linked to the geometry of the particles in question. Furthermore, we discovered that the shear thickening threshold exhibits a linear correlation with the viscosity of the matrix fluid, which can be seen as a manifestation of a broader universal phenomenon. Additionally, we found that the geometry of the particles plays a significant role in determining both the stress increase and the threshold at the onset of shear thickening. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the jamming transition that occurs during shear thickening can be understood in terms of the competition between two timescales: the rotation time of the particles and the time required for the formation of a nearest neighbor pair. This understanding provides a new framework for addressing this complex phenomenon and has important implications for our understanding of the dynamics that govern particle interactions in crowded environments. This knowledge of particle dynamics may also be applied to systems involving soft particles such as ellipsoids, where the effect of shear thickening is influenced by the balance between rotation time, approach time, and deformation. Our study shows that in a bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet, low-lying triplon
excitations may offer a path to achieving supersolid and superfluid phases, which
could be determined by varying an artificial spin-orbit coupling in the two
layers. When this coupling is insufficient, we predict the existence of a curved
superfluid phase. Conversely, a strong coupling results in a complex and curved
superfluid phase. Moreover, we demonstrate that an inhomogeneous magnetic
field can isolate a triplon-filled supersolid phase from its homogeneous
counterpart. Notably, lattice symmetry allows for the creation of a curved
superfluid phase at the expense of the triplon-filled supersolid phase. A
quantum Monte Carlo-deformation technique is employed to achieve these results. 
The deformed model matches its parent model with accuracy, as evidenced by a
comparison of their corresponding structure factors and energy spectra. A triplon
filled supersolid state is expected to occur at relatively high magnetic field
strengths along the x-y directions, whereas a curved superfluid and supersolid
phases are anticipated at lower, anisotropic magnetic field conditions. 
Experimental probing of these predictions is advised using NMR, Raman, and
muon precession relaxation experiments.
