Current Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) primarily focus on generating single, high-quality images or text samples, but they don't address the fundamental issue of creating sparse text documents that are common in real-world applications. To address this challenge, we introduce the SparseGAN model, which builds upon traditional GANs by incorporating a unique framework that leverages an over-complete code to represent the noise input, thereby enabling the generation of text data with predetermined number of active words. By applying an entropy-based penalty to the generator's loss function, we can control the overall sparsity of the generated text. Moreover, a proposed Code Regulator network codes the input data using the same over-complete code used by the generator, enabling efficient decoding and facilitating training via adversarial auxiliary auto-encoders. By implementing a code regularization technique, we can enforce code sparsity and develop a code-based sparsity mechanism that automates the selection of active words. Ultimately, we demonstrate SparseGAN's efficacy by applying it to removing unnecessary words from existing texts and generating new descriptive captions for data sets with limited annotation. Experimental results indicate that SparseGAN achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Modality-bridging Task (MT) and outperforms alternative sparsity-inducing models on the Columbia Image Dataset (CID) and the 15SemCor dataset. Source code is available at https://github.com/hk82/SparseGAN.

Evaluating soccer team performance for betting purposes or sports analysis usually focuses on advanced metrics like expected goal models. To ensure these assessments remain accessible and easy to apply across different datasets, we've developed a generalized framework for measuring defense based on probability estimates of conceding goals. To test this method's effectiveness, we analyzed team statistics from the UEFA Euro 2020 and 2022 tournaments using this framework and compared its results to the expected goal model. According to our analysis, there was a strong correlation between the two approaches in identifying the best defensive teams. However, our method yielded more consistent rankings throughout the tournament. Notably, both approaches ranked England's defense as the best, but our method ranked France's defense second while the expected goal model ranked Belgium's defense in the same spot. Our method also revealed hidden insights, such as Portugal's solid defense according to our analysis but not the expected goal model, and how both methods struggled to agree on the worst defensive teams. To further validate our approach, we conducted a simulation of the tournaments using our method and the expected goal model, and our analysis showed that our method performed better in predicting tournament outcomes. To explore how these methods perform at different stages of the tournament, we applied them to match data from the knockout rounds. Our analysis suggested that both approaches valued possession-based defenses more highly in these matches, and we found similar correlations between these methods and the total goals scored by each team. Our research provides a new perspective on measuring soccer team performance using advanced methods, and our findings can be applied to enhance sports analysis and betting strategies. Finally, we outline potential advancements to our method, including incorporating additional data and more complex defensive metrics, and we highlight the broader geographical interest in this research. This framework theoretics foundation provides a framework for developing computationally efficient algorithms, and a concrete implementation, the Concealed Parameter Linear Regression State Space model, is also analyzed through numerical simulations and a notable expansion of its model is proposed. This model's computation, however, is not feasible with current computational tools. A alternative, albeit suboptimal, algorithm for this model is also proposed and analyzed through numerical simulations. This methodic exploration of these approaches provides a clear path for developing algorithms that can handle hidden process alterations in state space models. A crucial role in this proof is identified for an independent, normally distributed vector that can be derived from a given matrix's individual spectral density subspaces. A key innovation in this work involves using independent, normally distributed random variables to construct the independent, normally distributed vector, as opposed to the standard approach of using standard Bernoulli distributed random variables. This extension facilitates the application of this result to a broader set of matrix-valued random variables, including those with non-positive semi-definite spectral density. A related consequence of this proof is the introduction of freely independent $n$-tuples of complex, normally distributed vectors. A related issue is the condition under which free independence and conditional independence are equivalent for complex, normally distributed vectors. A condition satisfying this equivalence is the vectors being normally distributed, as demonstrated by a specific example of power-free, complex, normally distributed vectors. We examine a degree 3 cover $f$: $\bar{X}$ $\to$ $X$ of a genus 1 curve $X$ over an algebraically closed field $k$. We show that if $X$ is non-hyperelliptic, the variety $P$ associated with the square of the Jacobian of $X$ and the pullback of its Jacobian under $f$, is isomorphic to an open part of the variety parametrizing genus 2 curves with a 2-fold cover. This connection enables us to establish a connection between the moduli space of genus 2 curves with a 2-fold cover and the variety $P$. If $X$ is a genus 1 curve that can be parameterized by a 2-fold cover of a genus 0 curve, we show that the variety $P$ is isomorphic to an open part of the variety parametrizing genus 0 curves with a degree 3 cover. This result generalizes a previous finding for a specific case. We also show that if $X$ is a genus 1 curve that can be parameterized by a 2-fold cover of a genus 3 curve, we can parameterize the variety $P$ as the intersection of two moduli spaces, one for genus 3 curves with a 2-fold cover and one for genus 0 curves with a degree 3 cover. These results provide a new perspective on the variety $P$ and its connection to the moduli spaces of genus 2 curves with a 2-fold cover, genus 0 curves with a degree 3 cover, and genus 3 curves with a 2-fold cover. We also show that the dimension of $P$ is 5 over fields of characteristic not 2. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the adoption of advanced computing technologies, enabling people to work remotely. This trend is expected to continue in the future, influencing how large-scale user centers design their remote systems. Here, we discuss the value of integrating artificial intelligence into remote infrastructure management to boost productivity and efficiency. By automating routine tasks and providing intuitive interfaces, AI can free up human resources for more complex issues, thereby improving problem-solving collaboration between humans and machines. We explore examples of pre-existing AI solutions that can be applied to various use cases and highlight a few prominent ones such as HPC-Optimize, a tool for automatically optimizing application performance across different supercomputers. We also introduce a few novel AI solutions including one that expedites the process of reproducing scientific experiments by automatically identifying performance bottlenecks and suggesting pre-processing data adjustments to achieve desired outcomes on HPC systems. Another one is a project that leverages self-supervised learning to develop accurate models for predicting application performance, a challenge that has traditionally been addressed through benchmarking. In the early 20th century, Adriaan van Maanen collaborated with Johan Jacobus van Rhijn and S. van Ash on a project to map the stellar populations of four specific areas of the sky. Following Van Rhijn's appointment as director of Kapteyn's Observatory in 1937, the project's findings were published under his name right before the second edition of "The Observatory" was printed. Van Rhijn made significant contributions to the field of astronomical research, particularly in the areas of proper motions, galaxy statistics and the local cosmic environment. His work laid the groundwork for a more in-depth study of the specific areas and his retirement in 1958 marked the end of an important era at Kapteyn's Observatory. A new initiative was launched in 2007 to revive the project that had been dormant for nearly five decades. A digital archive storing all the data collected since the 1930s has been established and a team of researchers is once again studying the stars in the selected areas with a more advanced approach using a wider range of observational data. Comparing their results with the earlier findings obtained during the 1930s-1940s has revealed some initial interesting discoveries. For example, the abundance of heavy elements in one of the areas called "S106" was found to be significantly higher than initially estimated and there are also indications that the rotation periods of stars are being affected by the presence of a binary companion. More in-depth analysis of all the data collected since the 1930s will likely yield a more substantial number of significant discoveries. Presently, all the available information on the stellar populations of the selected areas is being made public through a series of digital charts available on the project's website. These digital charts display all the stars that could be identified since the 1930s along with their photographic magnitudes, colors and derived parameters such as mass, size, temperature and the presence of a binary companion. They provide a valuable resource for any researcher who needs to cross-correlate the results obtained from the analysis of the stellar populations with other studies of these specific areas of the sky. They can be used to select the most suitable targets for a more in-depth analysis using a variety of observational techniques such as spectroscopy, polarimetry and interferometry and they can also be employed to enhance the effectiveness of astronomical surveys like the Hipparcos mission and the upcoming Gaia mission. Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To further our understanding of phylogenetic networks in general, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of six popular tools that utilize maximum likelihood principles to infer these networks from aligned DNA sequences. This study involves evaluating the theoretical capabilities of these tools, as well as a practical assessment using real and simulated data sets. Our results highlight the unique characteristics of each tool's inferred network distribution and reveal that some tools can accurately reproduce random tree topologies, while others exhibit a bias toward preferring tree-like structures even when given unstructured DNA sequences. These findings underscore the significance of selecting the appropriate tool for the type of data being analyzed and highlight the value of employing multiple methods for network inference. Our study also demonstrates that several of these tools can successfully deliver high-quality networks that accurately reflect real data networks, as evidenced by their ability to integrate adjacent gene trees into networks and remove unnecessary reticulations. However, there is a need for further development in some tools, such as those dealing with polyploidy and ancient recombination events. Our research lays the groundwork for a more in-depth comparison of these tools, one that could involve assessing the tools' sensitivity to different network structures and their ability to recover true histories in the presence of noise. Ultimately, this study emphasizes the importance of thorough testing before each new phylogenetic network inference tool is publicly released. Our investigation involves a substantial dataset of 96 real DNA data sets and over 10,000 simulated datasets, and our results show that the choice of tool significantly depends on the type of data being analyzed, with different tools being preferred for real data, unsampled ancestral recombination graphs, and specific types of simulated data sets. Our study also introduces a new metric called the "reticulation index," which measures the level of reticulation in networks and provides a useful framework for comparing the performance of different network inference tools. Our study is significant because it sets a high standard for the evaluation of new phylogenetic network inference tools and establishes a valuable network data repository that can be used for further comparison and testing of these tools. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing requires topological error correction, involving a large number of qubits undergoing frequent measurements to encode a single qubit, including a network of qubits measuring parity information in a surface code. To achieve high performance in this process using near-term quantum computers, we propose the use of reinforcement learning to optimize the sequence of quantum gate commands, or coders, necessary for surface code decoding, particularly for the 5x5 grid commonly used for catalina codes. By framing the coding process as a problem of partial feedback, where the coder must make decisions based on the overall code's state rather than individual qubit measurements, we developed a method of training quantum computers to generate optimal coders using reinforcement learning. When tested against random coders and qubit error scenarios, the performance of these learned coders showed significant improvements, with benefits including reduced qubit utilization, lower operational overhead, and enhanced resistance to certain types of errors. However, their effectiveness also depends on the specific error scenario and quantum computer architecture. To overcome the challenge of training on limited data available during quantum computation, we explored the use of pre-trained coders and different learning algorithms, with an appendix providing further details on these experiments. Despite the advances made, further optimization is necessary to fully integrate this coder into the quantum error correction process, particularly when incorporating the feedback provided by qubit measurement outcomes. To this end, we examined potential ways to modify the coder's learning algorithm to account for this additional information, with potential solutions such as introducing a memory component to the coder, but a more comprehensive approach is necessary to fully integrate this coder into the quantum error correction process. With near-term quantum computers focusing on sequence-dependent error rates and limited coders, further work is also needed to integrate this approach with the broader quantum error correction pipeline. Collection of data, coder training, and execution of coded quantum algorithms should be performed as interconnected modules rather than standalone processes. Furthermore, incorporating different types of quantum error models and simulating the performance of this coder on real quantum architectures are also necessary steps in this research. With these extensions in mind, we hope this study paves the way for further exploration of coders as a means of managing quantum error, with potential applications extending beyond near-term quantum computers, particularly when used for machine learning and other sequence-dependent quantum applications. Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements of an output signal. Although this approach offers superior precision, it requires complex state preparations and delicate control over the measurement process. An alternative method, known as quantum leap metrology, bypasses the need for sophisticated state preparation and direct measurement control. This method leverages a two-cavity network to amplify the precision of measuring an unknown phase shift automatically, following the contamination of an entangled state of two atoms. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in dual-cavity networks, highlighting the ability to accurately determine phase shifts at high speeds. Notably, we show that quantum leap metrology can achieve similar precision improvements as other quantum-enhanced metrology methods, albeit with a much simpler implementation. Furthermore, this method allows for the estimation of multiple unknowns concurrently, giving it a significant advantage over other quantum-enhanced metrology methods that require complex state preparations and direct measurement control. An application of this method to the measurement of magnetic fields in free fall demonstrates its potential to contribute to the sensitivity of such measurements. Overall, quantum leap metrology offers a breakthrough in precision measurement, achievable with basic state preparations and without the need for direct control over the measurement process. This method serves as an example of how quantum physics can be exploited to enhance the precision of measurements automatically. Our study investigates the interaction of jets with medium using direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Due to the virtual nature of photons, they interact with hadrons only through the medium's collective motion, allowing us to bypass medium-protein interactions that complicate interpretations. Our research extends the study of photon-hadron correlations to higher $p_T$ and includes additional hadron species. In $d$$+$Au collisions at 200 GeV, we observe photon-hadron $p_T$ correlations that reflect the movement of the Au medium as hadrons are emitted in the forward direction. This result is used to place constraints on jet-protein interactions in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au collisions, with findings indicating significant jet energy loss and medium modification in the midrapidity region. Furthermore, we observe significant differences in photon-hadron $p_T$ correlations in Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions at the same $N_{\rm part}$ values, with ratios of Au$+$Au to $d$$+$Au correlations increasing with hadron $p_T$. This suggests an interaction between the jet and medium that results in the deposition of extra medium energy in the direction transverse to the hadron momentum in $d$$+$Au, likely caused by the creation of a quark-gluon plasma in nose-beyond-tail collisions. The implications of these findings on jet energy loss and medium response in Au$+$Au collisions at midrapidity are significant, with additional evidence of jet-quenched medium response in Au$+$Au at midrapidity. A detailed analysis of photon-hadron $p_T$ correlations in Au$+$Au collisions reveals a medium modification that varies with both photon and hadron $p_T$, with ratios of Au$+$Au to $d$$+$Au correlations dependent on hadron type. This result highlights the complex nature of jet-protein interactions in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au collisions at midrapidity. A qualitative comparison of medium modification in midrapidity and semi-central Au$+$Au collisions reveals distinct characteristics, with implications for our understanding of jet-protein interactions in medium with varying density. This study solidifies the value of direct photon-hadron correlations as a primary method for assessing jet-medium interactions and lays the groundwork for further investigation using the PHENIX detector at RHIC and the JETMAPS dataset

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when dynamic interactions between rigid bodies and deformable environments are involved. This study focuses on a single-legged hopper interacting with a nonlinear, viscous, and memoryless ground surface. Initially, the model is simplified to accommodate linear ground characteristics, enabling an in-depth analysis of the critical conditions necessary for stable single-legged hopping dynamics. When the ground responds linearly, there is no influence on the hopper's equilibrium points or stability near those points. However, when the ground reacts nonlinearly, the possibility of stable dynamic hopping exists only when the friction threshold is exceeded by an additional factor of one plus the square of the hopper's natural frequency, obtained from a dimensionless form of the model. When the ground's response is linear in proportion to the depth of penetration, the condition for stable dynamic hopping is (sqrt(3)/2)^4, or approximately 1.28, which can be improved to 1.41 by increasing the foot's stiffness four times. This research provides a framework for optimizing single-legged hopping on yielding terrain through the identification of specific parameters that can be adjusted to achieve more stable dynamic hopping. When applied to walking on yieldable surfaces, this knowledge could be useful in developing control systems that localize similar frequency-based relationships across the multiple legs used in bipedal locomotion. Effective information management relies on accurate understanding of negation in text, a skill that has not been thoroughly assessed in existing reading comprehension benchmarks. To fill this gap, we introduce CONDAQA, a diverse Negation Reading Comprehension Dataset featuring 5,192 human-labeled questions. These questions require reasoners to grasp the impact of negation on the overall meaning and are answerable with either "Supported" or "Refuted", depending on the presence or absence of negation in the referenced text passages. CONDAQA covers a range from simple to complex and incorporates various negation expressions to test a model's robustness. When tested on the set of 504 validated pairs, our proposed method achieved a notable improvement over baseline models, outperforming them by a significant margin. However, we discovered that even high-performing models tended to perform subpar when confronted with more intricate negation expressions or longer passages. This insight suggests that there is still a need for innovation in modeling the interpretation of negation and suggests that multi-negation scenario studies could provide valuable insights. Additionally, our results on the challenges of CONDAQA have implications for other datasets that may rely heavily on the understanding of negation and prompted the creation of a new dataset called Negation Prompt Analysis Dataset (NPAD). This new dataset comprises a variety of prompts that either do or do not incorporate negation and was used to guide the development of a new set of models designed to better comprehend the impact of negation on text. These models' performance will be subject to a thorough evaluation against the CONDAQA dataset. We have established that a compact, uniformly parabolic manifold, which diminishes its Ricci tensor and has constant scalar curvature, is geodesically complete and thus allows for the application of the Maximum Principle to partial differential equations. As a result, we derive that its distance function is an harmonic function, and consequently, we can prove that the manifold itself is geodesically complete in the hyperbolic sense. This completeness in the hyperbolic sense has the consequence that the manifold's distance function is actually bounded, which in turn implies that the manifold itself is geodesically complete in the classical sense. We demonstrate the utility of this completeness in the hyperbolic sense by showing that a particular differential equation admits a solution within this manifold. The technique we use to achieve this completeness in the hyperbolic sense may also be employed to prove a more general Liouville Theorem for a broader class of manifolds. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common for many question answering tasks to leverage external knowledge. However, the vast majority of existing approaches solely utilize pre-trained language models to retrieve knowledge, without considering the semantic relationships between knowledge and question. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel Coarse-to-Precise (C2P) framework to efficiently explore semantic relationships in the knowledge retrieval process. This framework is built on top of a dual-retrieval structure, where it performs a initial coarse retrieval to obtain a set of relevant knowledge snippets, and then refines its search within this subset by incorporating semantic clues from the question. To effectively learn from these clues, we incorporate a question knowledge graph, and introduce a graph attention-based encoder to embed both the question and knowledge graph into semi-meaningful representations. These representations are then used to compute a clue distribution that guides the precise retrieval process. We evaluate the C2P framework on the Open-domain Commonsense Question Answering task, achieving a significant improvement over the baseline models and establishing a new state-of-the-art on the COCO dataset with an F1 score of 41.3%. The code is available at: https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-CLG/tree/main/c2p.

This allows us to establish an important relationship between the metric components and the nonisotropic pressure field. Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning is crucial for developing trusted interactions between autonomous agents in companies that heavily rely on data privacy and security. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on counterfactual learning from carefully curated contrasting data, our method efficiently learns from positive trajectories alone. Without the need to label contrasting data or estimate the individual agents' rewards, our approach leverages the underlying structure of multi-agent reinforcement learning to generate contrastive contrasting trajectories directly from the available data. We establish a theoretical framework that bounds the generalization error of our estimator and the expected return of the learned policy. Our experiments validate our algorithm's effectiveness and efficiency on complex scenarios, including power management in data centers and aerial traffic scenarios. Analysis of optical spectra throughout the event allowed researchers to study the movement of the nova ejecta and surrounding pre-explosive disk. They found that the pre-explosive disk extended beyond the solar system's orbital radius and consisted of material accumulated over many years. This, in turn, implies that classical novae generally undergo a significant explosion force that propels a substantial amount of pre-explosive material into interstellar space. Researchers typically measure the progress of their field through output metrics and the advancement of overall knowledge, often represented by the categorization of scientific papers. To explore this assumption, we conduct a comprehensive examination across multiple fields using both automated and manual knowledge bases. The outcome indicates that the correlation between output and knowledge progression varies greatly among disciplines. For instance, the relationship between quantum output and knowledge progression is closely aligned, whereas there is a significant disparity in classical physics. Our analysis based on diverse indicators also reveals distinct patterns. Notably, the correlation holds strong in fields like computer science and biology but dissipates in social sciences, physics, mathematics, chemistry, and engineering. Our study implies that valuing output over knowledge progression or vice versa in scientific assessment needs to be reevaluated and adapted to the specific characteristics of each field. Furthermore, we propose a new, more flexible framework that accounts for both output and knowledge progression in equal measure. This framework enables a nuanced assessment of scientific progress across different disciplines. Our results demonstrate its utility and suggest that it can be applied to a broad spectrum of fields. However, there are instances where this approach still falls short in accurately capturing the progress made in a particular field. For those cases, we propose additional indicators that combine output and knowledge progression using our framework. Our exploration of these indicators reveals that they can be quite diverse. For instance, the combined approach aligns with the expert's assessment in the field of quantum physics but yields a result that doesn't hold up to scrutiny in classical physics. To gain a deeper understanding of our findings, we examine the discrepancy between output and knowledge progression in detail. We discovered that the knowledge base used for measurement had a significant impact on the results. Furthermore, the outcome was also influenced by the methodology employed to calculate the output and the structure of the taxonomy that defined the advancement of knowledge. To get a better sense of these findings, we conduct a similar analysis on a smaller scale using a reduced taxonomic tree. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation in developing and testing these agents has been the slow speed at which text games are interactive - a major hindrance being the current capability of computer processors to process only up to 10,000 actions per second in typical text-based games.
This slowdown hampers both the training and testing of sophisticated agents by limiting them to simple environments and only using basic skills.
To address this constraint, we introduce TextWorldExpress, a high-performance version of TextWorld that achieves action processing speeds of over one million actions per second, allowing for more sophisticated agents to be tested in more complex scenarios. This advancement in technology is being made available to the public to accelerate the development of innovative methods for training and evaluating virtual agents. We also provide initial research into defining quantitative metrics to assess the realism of text-based games and showcase the performance gains that can be achieved with modern computer hardware. Finally, we invite the community to contribute their knowledge and expertise to a public forum to shape the future direction of text-based games. This initiative includes an open-source repository of pre-trained models that can process text at incredible speeds, along with suggestions on how to integrate your own expert knowledge into these models. This integrated knowledge can be used to create realistic scenarios for testing the abilities of virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge. We hope that these accelerated text-based games, along with expertly trained models and challenging scenarios, will contribute meaningfully to the advancement of artificial intelligence. This work is presented at the 28th Conference on Artificial Intelligence, where it received the award for Best Application Paper. This achievement would not have been possible without the support of NVIDIA, Google, and Microsoft, which provided access to cutting-edge hardware and cloud services that enabled us to push the boundaries of what is possible with text-based games. This work is a collaboration between multiple researchers from different institutions. We are open to the inclusion of additional researchers who share our passion for artificial intelligence. This work was done with the support of multiple universities and research centers. This tensor transformation method can be implemented using a relatively simple and low-power hardware design consisting of a memory-efficient tensor core and two LSTM modules. The paper addresses the issue of whether the next term in a sequence of function compositions can be determinately found from previous terms, a question initially raised by the mathematician and computer scientist, Mel Hampson, in the 1940s. Although Hampson's initial method was later disproven, the question remains relevant today. This paper presents several novel approaches to resolving this issue for specific types of functions, including polynomials and exponential functions. In the case of polynomials, it is shown that if the degree of the polynomial is prime, then the next term in the sequence can be determined uniquely. Additionally, the paper identifies patterns in sequences of composite functions over the integers, and it presents a general formula for the nth term of a sequence of composite functions of degree 'p' for prime p. This formula was initially discovered through the use of integer arithmetic, but it has since been extended to include the use of 'p' distinct real roots. This extension allows for the determination of the next term in a sequence of composite functions that has a rational root. Furthermore, the paper presents several examples of sequences of composite functions with irrational roots, and it identifies patterns in these sequences as well. Finally, this paper also explores relationships between sequences of composite functions and the concept of infinite sets, and it raises several additional questions related to the issue it addresses. In the case of exponential functions, it is shown that if an exponential function is expressed in a specific form, then the next term in a sequence of its composites can be determined uniquely. This determination allows for the analysis of local behavior, but it does not provide a full picture of the sequence's global behavior. Notably, this paper does not address the issue of whether the next term in a sequence of composite functions can be determined uniquely for all functions, but it does show that this condition is satisfied for the classes of functions it considers, including polynomials and exponential functions. This satisfaction implies that these types of functions have a property referred to as'recursive simplicity', and this property allows for the efficient computation of their iterates using a limited number of computer memory cells. This property is significant because it distinguishes these types of functions from other types of functions, and it makes them suitable for use in computer programs that involve the computation of iterates and other sequences of functions. Finally, this property is also the key to unlocking further mathematical generalizations and to providing solutions to otherwise intractable problems, as demonstrated by the examples and the questions raised in this paper. Topological quantum error correction codes such as the toric code have been shown to be highly resistant to random errors, allowing quantum computations to be performed reliably. Topological quantum computations using stabilizer codes can be employed with a single parity-check iteration, serving as a foundation for our further discussions. Building upon this foundation, we develop a method to analyze the performance of quantum error correction protocols using classical statistical mechanics techniques. By applying this method to the study of classical toric codes modelled after the Ising model, we gain insight into the boundary regions where quantum computations become practical. We utilize a novel mixed finite element approach to analyze single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous medium, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, leading to separate treatments in our numerical model. For the $d$-dimensional space, we implement a mixed finite element method based on subdomain techniques, while for the $d+1$-dimensional space, we employ a hybrid $hp$-finite element approach, both resulting in a consistent linear system for solving pressure across the fractures. However, due to the varying pressures on the two faces of each fracture, we incorporate an additional compatibility condition, effectively doubling the number of unknowns by one for each fracture. Ultimately, our approach facilitates a computationally efficient way to account for the impact of fractures on Darcy flow using mixed finite elements. This method holds potential for expanding to account for non-linear flows and interface movements. This research builds upon previous work by J. A. Munar, in which a $hp$-finite element approach was tested against experimental data of flow through a single fracture with a complex geometry. This new approach has been successfully applied to simulate the drainage problem around a horizontal fracture and compared against analytical and semi-analytical solutions. Additionally, it has been used to model flow through multiple fractures, one of which is complex in geometry, and a comparison is made with an existing method, revealing a notable improvement in the accuracy of this approach. This research has important implications for the optimization of water injection patterns used in the recovery of oil in fractured reservoirs. This method has also been used in conjunction with the program OSCAR to generate models of flow through complex fractures. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. This dataset is distinct from datasets used for classification tasks, such as SBUv2 and TreeBank, and includes a universally accepted set of discourse indicators that can be clustered into eight categories. Intrinsic neural networks are frequently employed as a basic framework for understanding brain function, but their simplicity may not accurately reflect the intricate interactions between neurons and the varied electrical states of synapses. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a new model that incorporates a detailed biological framework, including multiple types of synaptic transmitters and the associated molecular processes, such as long-term potentiation and the interaction between heterosynaptic facilitation. This integrated network is an extension of previous work by Votsmeier and Sebastianard, and our simulations demonstrate that it exhibits dynamic properties characteristic of intrinsic neural networks. This biologically complex network is an overview of a cortical microcircuit, comprising different types of excitatory and inhibitory neurons that represent various cellular components with distinct properties. Our research aims to explore whether a simple neural connection pattern can produce a range of behaviors observed in intrinsic neural networks when coupled with the underlying biological processes of synapses and neurons. Our findings suggest that indeed this is possible. To take the model to the next level, we plan to investigate its application to a range of behavioral patterns observed in intrinsic neural networks. Our analysis reveals that the optimal solutions' geodesic paths exhibit convex properties within this manifold. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. The reliability of these systems in the real world is being threatened by the increasing prevalence of hardware anomalies triggered by natural flaws in electronic components, environmental stressors and energetic attacks. The existing approach of using robust neural networks designed with intentionally introduced errors to enhance tolerance has its limitations due to the significant overhead in model size and computational complexity. This research introduces a novel technique called activation interval supervision which identifies and rectifies faulty neurons during training. The proposed method recognizes faulty activations by analyzing the distributions of intermediate output layers and normalizes them to conform to a specific exponential distribution. The implementation of a practical method based on reversible normalization enables the recovery of original data distribution without affecting the performance. Experimental results show that this technique achieves comparable accuracy with only a minimal percentage of reduced accuracy when comparing to traditional cross entropy loss training. The proposed method also offers computational savings of at least 1.5 times when compared to robust training for different deep neural network architectures. This research provides a preliminary security case for activation interval supervision but further research is needed to fully formalize the security aspect. The proposed method has been experimentally validated on a variety of datasets including MNIST, CIFAR10 and SVHN. The results show a minimal accuracy decrease of 2% when comparing to traditional training and confirm that activation interval supervision is an efficient method for detecting and rectifying faulty neurons during the training of deep neural networks. This paper proposes a novel approach to construct a shared semantic space for multiple languages. Unlike previous methods that utilized single learning algorithms for multiple languages or similar methods that employed cross-language learning for single languages, our approach leverages single-language word representation techniques while ensuring the resulting representations are cross-language compatible. We achieve this by clustering words in each language and mapping the learned representations to a shared space where the clusters correspond to the same semantic concepts across languages. We utilize the K-Means algorithm to cluster words within each language and apply a consensus algorithm to ensure the representations are cluster-consistent. Our method improves the quality of shared semantic spaces by reducing both intra-cluster variance and cross-language misalignment. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying the shared space to three cross-language tasks: word translation, sentiment analysis, and text classification. Our results show that our method produces accurate word translations and achieves comparable or better performance on sentiment analysis and text classification when compared to state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, our method allows for the incorporation of additional languages without the need for retraining the model in each language. We also release two cluster-consistent word representation datasets that can be utilized for evaluating our approach. The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains glaring errors in its annotated data. These flaws significantly impede the performance improvement of models. To break through this limitation, we introduce the revised ASSIST dataset, derived from MultiWOZ 2.0 with the following key improvements: incorrect labels have been corrected, redundant information removed, and ambiguous labels redefined using additional dataset analysis. Furthermore, we introduce a new assessment metric called Inference-Based Accuracy, which mimics real-world scenarios by assuming annotators are human dialogue state trackers. This metric highlights the common issue of over-accurate model performance when evaluated against their training data. To address this, we introduce three additional evaluation metrics, along with three challenging evaluation scenarios, to provide a comprehensive assessment of dialogue state tracking models. Our findings indicate current state-of-the-art models perform exceptionally well on conventional evaluation metrics but struggle with accuracy in real-world scenarios. Hence, we introduce an additional comparison between models that achieve high scores on conventional metrics but fall short in actual performance. Our research discovers that these underperforming models exhibit a common characteristic: they tend to mistakenly include nonevent entities in the dialogue state track. This insight guides our proposal of a linear model that outperforms all previous state-of-the-art models on the revised ASSIST dataset. Our work sets a new benchmark for the community to build upon, and our findings shed light on the critical issue of label imperfection in dialogue state tracking. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that significant room exists for further improvement in this field. System models are tested on an online platform to gather more practical assessment metrics. In late October 2019, violent protests broke out in Chile, leading to prolonged civil unrest and widespread disruption.  To understand the dynamics of this event, we developed an epidemiological non-local model to simulate the spread of information and the resulting behavioral changes among the population.  The model accounts for both local influence, such as word-of-mouth interactions, and long-range connections, representing the impact of regional changes in social media trends.  By applying this approach to the Chilean protests, we were able to interpret the resulting mathematical equations and simulate the complex phenomena observed during this period.  Our simulations reveal that a combination of both local and non-local interactions is responsible for the rapid spread of information and the resulting temporal patterns in behavioral changes, as observed in real-world data.  Furthermore, we explore how different population responsiveness to changes in regional trends shapes the dynamics of this event, and our findings have implications for monitoring and predicting similar types of social unrest.  Additionally, we apply a similar approach to analyzing video views on YouTube, demonstrating that this model can be applicable across different platforms and populations.  By incorporating real-world data and a numerical method to solve the equations, we obtain simulations that accurately match the observed patterns in real-world data, providing a theoretical framework for understanding the complex dynamics of social unrest in the digital age.  We believe that this approach can be used to study other complex phenomena resulting from the interaction of local and non-local influences in social networks. Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure a crucial parameter $r$ with high precision, however a significant challenge lies ahead. Delensing, the process to extract a primordial signal buried under another signal caused by gravitational lensing, is key. To improve this process beyond traditional quadratic estimators which may not be sufficient, the next generation experiments could potentially benefit from more sophisticated methods such as a maximum a posteriori estimator or even a machine learning approach. Using a neural network to model an estimator that takes into account both lensing and primordial power spectra, we found it was possible to achieve a precision on $r$ estimation of $\sigma(r) = 3.96 \times 10^{-9}$ with a total of $10^5$ simulations for an ideal experiment, and with a realistic experiment such as CMB-S4 it yielded $\sigma(r) = 4.53 \times 10^{-9}$. This suggests a machine learning approach could be an effective way to improve $r$ estimation in the future. Additionally we found that when estimating $r$ in the presence of a known primordial tensor fraction, a neural network was able to achieve a similar or in some cases better precision than an estimator that assumes no primordial lensing, and also that a model that takes into account an unknown primordial scalar fraction did not have a significant impact on the estimation of $r$. Lastly as the code that implements the neural network is openly available, it could serve as a starting point for any exploration of neural network driven delensing in the future. Converting ancient music notes into audible sound is a challenging Music Information Retrieval (MIR) task, primarily due to a lack of well-organized data. One key step in this process involves automatically transcribing keyboard recordings, which can be accomplished by a technique called Source Separation. In this study, we propose a semi-supervised Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (CNMF) method to execute this task. This approach builds upon the established multilinear factorization model and adapts it for processing continuous audio recordings represented as 3D matrices. By incorporating a constrained optimization process and an alternative update rule, our model surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques, including both supervised and unsupervised methods. We also utilize a novel initialization strategy to enhance the model's performance in real-world applications. Notably, our approach has the unique benefit of processing recordings that include multiple overlapping sounds. We initiate evaluations using a newly collected and publicly accessible dataset comprising seven hours of recorded organ music with accurate transcriptions. Our results show significant improvement over existing methods, with an overall accuracy of 84.5%. This represents a notable increase from the previous state-of-the-art technique and confirms the effectiveness of CNMF for this specific task. However, CNMF's performance still declines when applied to recordings featuring piano music, indicating a potential need for further optimization. Ultimately, our proposed approach holds promise for the development of more sophisticated music retrieval tools. To facilitate this progress, we release an improved version of the publicly accessible dataset containing additional piano recordings with accurate transcriptions. This dataset, now comprising over 5 hours of recorded organ and piano music, is available for download at the provided URL. By initiating evaluations using this dataset and a newly introduced evaluation metric called Mean Ranks, we hope to contribute to the development of more robust music retrieval methods. Furthermore, we plan to build upon these experiments by exploring further optimizations and other music retrieval applications. We anticipate that our proposed approach will serve as a foundational model for these initiatives. The detection of gravitational waves (GWs) by the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) opens up new avenues for astrophysics, allowing for unprecedented access to neutron star-black hole (NS-BH) events. However, the extraction of valuable information from GW signals is a complex task due to their noise and the numerous parameters involved, often requiring significant amounts of computational resources. Traditional methods based on semi-kernel mutual information (MKI) have struggled to achieve high accuracy in the classification of these events. We introduce a novel multi-task deep learning framework known as the GW-Net, which leverages a combination of convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks to accurately identify and classify GW signals from NS-BH mergers. We employ the LIGO detection bank's parameter space grid, consisting of over 3,000 unique combinations of binary neutron star, NS-BH, and BH-BH merger parameters, to train our model. We achieve exceptional results on the test dataset, obtaining a 99.98% accuracy rate on event classification and a 98.13% accuracy rate on mass estimation. These advancements position our deep learning approach as a cutting-edge solution for processing large sets of GW data. Furthermore, this work lays the groundwork for further exploration in the field. We make the GW-Net code publicly available for reproducibility purposes and to facilitate potential extensions to other multi-task learning applications. Nonetheless, our study suggests that deep learning methods face challenges when adapting to new datasets, as demonstrated by our experiments with a smaller subset of the NS-BH data. For mobile robots to successfully navigate through unfamiliar environments independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One approach that holds promise is the use of games that incorporate multiple sensory modalities, as they have the ability to naturally inspire curiosity through their puzzles and mysteries.  By investigating the dynamics of curiosity in a small group of students playing such a game, we have identified the conditions that lead to an increase in curiosity levels.  Our findings indicate that advances in programming technologies such as agents, physics engines, and multi-agent systems can be leveraged to create more complex and realistic games that stimulate curiosity.  By integrating multiple sensory modalities, we have developed a scoring system that encourages curiosity-driven behavior by rewarding students for asking questions.  Our research has resulted in a theoretical model that describes the dynamics of curiosity in this setting, and we have explored several ways to personalize the learning experience using statistical methods.  Our study has implications for the design of more effective learning environments that promote curiosity in a variety of settings, and it has sparked a new research direction that focuses on the emotional aspects of learning.  By investigating the complex interplay between different emotions, we have developed a new theoretical framework that has the potential to address some of the world's most pressing challenges, such as improving learning outcomes, promoting creativity, and fostering a more empathetic and innovative society.  This thesis has provided a clear roadmap for the next set of research projects, and it has given some initial answers to the questions that were initially posed at the beginning of this study.  However, many more questions remain to be addressed, and it is our hope that this work will inspire a new generation of researchers to continue down this innovative path. While Gaussian processes provide an effective way to model unknown relationships, the traditional approach relies on the use of squared exponential kernels, which can be challenging to apply to large data sets due to their computationally expensive implementation. The recent development of matrix Gaussian processes, such as Mat\'ern Gaussian processes, presents a more efficient alternative, based on the use of power exponential kernels that reduce the need for expensive scalar inversions. Although matrix Gaussian processes have been successful in various applications, their potential for handling complex data sets with irregular structures has yet to be explored. The aim of this work is to introduce matrix Gaussian processes as a novel approach for analyzing interdependent data, enabling the development of statistical models that can handle non-stationary relationships, missing values, and time series data, as well as to showcase its applicability using real-world datasets. While DNA is commonly considered a reliable source for identifying cell populations, it's not always feasible to obtain DNA samples, making nucleus detection crucial. However, existing methods lack the necessary precision to accurately identify nuclei within complex cellular environments. To address this issue, we propose a new dual-stage convolutional network called W-Net that combines semi-supervised learning with optimized features to enhance detection performance. Initially, the network uses a simple classifier to eliminate obvious non-nucleus regions, thereby reducing unnecessary computation and focusing the attention on high-priority areas. This is followed by an in-depth detection stage that utilizes refined features to locate potential nuclei within the optimized mask regions. Through extensive testing on two substantial datasets, we demonstrate that our proposed W-Net outperforms the current state-of-the-art models with improved accuracy and efficiency. Notably, W-Net achieves exceptional results on the challenging Lymph node dataset with a remarkable 32.3% reduction in false positives compared to the top-performing baseline model. Our model's exceptional performance paves the way for further research in multi-task learning to integrate nucleus detection with other analysis tasks. Additionally, we make the following contributions to the field: (1) we present two crucial datasets consisting of 50,000 annotations, along with detailed data preparation protocols; (2) we introduce a challenging multi-stage task for detecting nuclei, along with applicable evaluation metrics; and (3) we make our proposed framework's code and implementation publicly available for reproducibility and future extensions. Despite its excellence, our proposed framework has room for improvement, especially in terms of preserving detected nucleus regions' spatial coherence. Through further research, we aim to integrate additional information about nucleus spatial organization to enhance the detection performance. One potential approach to achieve this is by incorporating multi-layer convolutional network to capture nucleus spatial relationships. However, this approach requires careful consideration of overfitting risks due to the introduction of additional network layers, along with suitable data augmentation strategies to expand the training dataset's diversity. Along with detecting nuclei within complex cellular environments, our proposed framework can be explored for integration with other analysis tasks, such as cell segmentation, tissue annotation, and DNA extraction, to name a few. Nevertheless, this would necessitate careful evaluation of all relevant performance metrics, along with tuning the framework's hyperparameters to optimize performance across all integrated tasks. Furthermore, our proposed dual-stage approach can be utilized as a pioneering work for investigating multi-task learning on complex cellular image analysis, even though it may require additional research to fully understand the implications of integrating multiple analysis tasks

Endogenous environments are those where external influences don't exist and all elements, including states and rewards, originate from internal mechanisms. In contrast, exogenous environments are shaped by external factors that aren't part of the system's dynamics. This distinction is crucial because many reinforcement learning theories assume endogenous settings by implying that states and rewards are generated randomly according to predefined probability distributions. However, this assumption isn't necessarily valid for all situations. If the system's state and reward functions can be determined, it's possible to use exploration data to a significant extent, as proven by a previous work. Here, we explore the reverse problem of identifying the system's underlying state and reward functions that give rise to the observed data. This problem can be solved by determining the minimal set of variables that fully captures the data's underlying structure. Furthermore, if the determined state and reward functions are identical, it implies that the environment is semi-encodable, a concept we introduce along with its two variants: fully encodable and unpredictably encodable. The former occurs when the state and reward functions are exactly the same, the latter when they aren't the same but there's still a clear connection between them, and the latter when no such connection exists. If the environment is semi-encodable, partial knowledge of the state and reward functions can be utilized to the user's advantage. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the limitation of this method lies in the requirement for two trained translator networks, one translating low-dose images to routine-dose images and the other routine-dose images to low-dose images, with the issue arising when applying this method in real-world scenarios where routine-dose images are often used as the starting point. To overcome this challenge, we propose an innovative adaptation of the cycleGAN method built on an adaptive instance normalization switchable cycleGAN framework. This research investigates an ideal fluid spacetime with a conformal Yamabe soliton, considering the relationship between its Ricci-Yamabe potential and the fluid's velocity field. By analyzing the soliton's equation, we find that a static, symmetric configuration meets the criteria, and we explore the conditions under which such a setup can maintain stability. Additionally, we identify that in the absence of the fluid's impact, a static, symmetric spacetime with a conformal Yamabe soliton is essentially a Ricci-Yamabe soliton on a manifold of constant curvature. Building on this, we demonstrate that in the absence of the fluid's velocity field, a Ricci-Yamabe soliton on a manifold of constant curvature results in a static, symmetric configuration. Furthermore, we establish that a compact, symmetric spacetime with a conformal Yamabe soliton can only sustain a non-zero fluid flow at velocities less than or equal to one. Constructively, we demonstrate that for any compact, symmetric spacetime and flow velocities less than one, there exists a static, symmetric configuration that can support the fluid flow. Finally, we prove that a compact, symmetric spacetime with a conformal Yamabe soliton and a non-zero fluid flow at velocities greater than one is collapsing. Moreover, we show that for any compact, symmetric spacetime and flow velocities greater than one, there exists a static, symmetric configuration that can support the fluid flow; this static configuration, however, will collapse. Building on these findings, we demonstrate that for any compact, symmetric spacetime and flow velocities less than one, there exists a static, symmetric configuration that can support the fluid flow, and this static configuration will not collapse. We perform a comprehensive analysis of effective on-site action for Mott insulators, focusing on the impact of hybridization and lattice effects on the behavior of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals in perovskite transition metal compounds. By incorporating the rotation symmetry of the cubic lattice into the calculation, we identify the unique "spin-orbital entanglement" of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ degrees of freedom. In particular, we reveal that the $t_{2g}$ doublet in 4d and 5d systems undergoes a phase transition from an isotropic state to an anisotropic one as the hybridization strength increases beyond a critical point. This transition has a marked effect on the materials' electronic properties and can result in the emergence of nematic electronic nematicity in 4d and 5d systems. In contrast, the $e_g$ doublet exhibits an isotropic phase for all hybridization strengths. Notably, this uniform behavior applies regardless of the metal's position in the periodic table or the presence of spin-orbit coupling. This unified understanding of the orbital structure can be utilized in the search for 4d and 5d Mott insulators that exhibit nematic electronic nematicity. Additionally, we expect this phenomenon to be induced by nematic spin-orbit coupling in 3d systems if the spin-orbit coupling is sufficient. Finally, we suggest that the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can result in the formation of nematic superconducting states. This prediction is supported by a numerical simulation of a 4d TiO$_6$ cluster, indicating that the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can facilitate the creation of nematic superconducting states. This finding holds important implications for the search for nematic superconductors in transition metal oxides.
